20483-artillery-through-the-ages-a-short:
Artillery Through the Ages gives a short illustrated history of cannon. It was made to help visitors at America's historic sites understand the guns they saw. Photographs show early nineteenth-century field guns and Civil War garrison pieces in place.

The captions name the shrines where the guns stand. Fort Pulaski keeps Civil War garrison guns, while Gettysburg holds field guns from the same war. Petersburg's park preserves its own batteries. The book traces cannon from crude early tubes to rifled artillery, tying each step to battlefields a reader can still walk.
20747-deaconesses-in-europe-and-their-le:
What place should women's church work hold? Deaconesses in Europe asks that hard question head on. The book asks what the early and medieval churches can teach on the point. It also asks if sisterhoods can grow without the harms of convent life.

European deaconess houses, where women served the sick and poor, fill the study. The author weighs their record and asks what America might safely copy. Church history, charity work, and women's roles meet in one debate. Readers get a clear window on a live church question of the late nineteenth century, argued with care.
21059-the-adventures-of-dick-maitland-a-:
Harry Collingwood sends a young doctor's apprentice from London's poor East End into unknown Africa in this adventure novel. Dick Maitland works for a kind doctor who treats the poor for almost nothing. When Dick's family fortunes fall, he works his passage to South Africa with no money at all.

On the ship Dick befriends a rich young man named Grosvenor, and the two set out to explore together. They meet peoples Collingwood had used in an earlier book, then seek a rumoured mysterious white race. Those people prove to be a lost tribe, and Dick returns home with valuable jewels.
21276-the-wars-between-england-and-ameri:
T. C. Smith, professor of American history at Williams College, published this short history in London in 1914. Twelve chapters run from the elements of antagonism in 1763 to the War of 1812 and a closing chapter on a century of peace. Parliamentary taxation, the disruption of the empire, and French intervention mark the first war.

Smith then follows the making of the United States, two periods of trade quarrels, and the war for sailors' rights and westward expansion. A bibliography and index close the book. Written on the eve of the First World War, it reads the old quarrels as a finished story between two now-friendly peoples.
21543-french-pathfinders-in-north-americ:
William Henry Johnson tells of France's explorers in French Pathfinders in North America, copyrighted in 1905. Jacques Cartier's portrait fronts the book, and seven full-page plates fill it. Johnson had already written on the world's discoverers and on pioneer Spaniards.

Early chapters treat the origins of the peoples called Indians and the Iroquois League. Then come Cartier in Canada, Ribaut at Port Royal, and Laudonnière on the St John's River. Champlain's work on the St Lawrence and the Great Lakes takes two chapters. Jesuit mission pioneers and later travellers carry the tale toward the French and Indian War.
21555-the-mission-or-scenes-in-africa:
An autumn expedition in 1828 opens Captain Marryat's The Mission, or Scenes in Africa, published in 1845. An elderly, infirm gentleman leads the party into the interior. One figure had made a fortune in India before ill health drove him home for a spell.

Marryat, who knew Africa from his own service, builds the tale on travel and mission work. Hunting, tribal politics, and the hardships of the road fill the scenes. The book was his twenty-second, late in a run of twenty-six. Its South African ground gives it a flavour unlike his sea tales, with the same gift for episode.
21682-the-field-and-garden-vegetables-of:
Fearing Burr Junior describes near eleven hundred vegetables in The Field and Garden Vegetables of America, issued at Boston in 1863. The full title promises each kind's size, form, colour, quality, and season. Hardiness, yield, and value for cultivation are set out for each.

Before Burr, such knowledge lay scattered in fragmentary sources, hard for beginners to find. His book gives directions for propagation, culture, and use in one place. Albert Fearing of Hingham, a backer of farming causes, receives the dedication. For gardeners and seed historians, the volume remains a rich record of American varieties before the modern seed trade.
21699-the-rover-of-the-andes-a-tale-of-a:
R. M. Ballantyne crosses South America in The Rover of the Andes, at about the latitude of Buenos Aires. A journey over the continent's heart carries the reader from chapter to chapter. Nasty folk and nasty happenings block the road, one by one overcome.

Ballantyne researched his settings by living among the men he wrote of, for weeks and months. Telegraph cables, lightships, lifeboats, and divers all drew that treatment from him. The Andes tale feels realistic, its editors say, though built of research and imagination. It carries the reader, panting for the next turn, right to the last chapter.
21766-ionica:
William Cory, born William Johnson in Devon in 1823, published the first Ionica in 1858, a slim green volume of forty-eight poems. A second set followed privately in 1877, printed without stops on the author's odd theory that spaces should mark the pauses. In 1891 he gathered most of both books, with new pieces, into the Ionica known today: eighty-five poems in all.

Arthur C. Benson adds a life of the poet and notes in this edition. Cory had been a master at Eton, and his lyrics carry a schoolmaster's love of Greek and Latin verse. The poems are brief, clear, and tender, often turned toward friendship, loss, and the shortness of life. Ionica became a quiet classic of Victorian lyric poetry.
22323-impressions-of-south-africa:
Impressions of South Africa records a close look at a troubled country in the 1890s. Its author wrote as political problems there grew acute. The closing chapter, written with events of early 1896 in view, still hoped for peace.

The writer believed those problems would be solved in a peaceable way. The qualities needed, he said, were tact, coolness, and patience. Patience, above all, was his repeated plea. That hope gives the book its value now. It shows how a thoughtful observer read South Africa just before war came. Readers can test his judgment against everything that followed in that decade.
22476-the-tale-of-mr-peter-brown-chelsea:
V. Sackville-West wrote The Tale of Mr. Peter Brown, Chelsea Justice, for the New Decameron. Her narrator reproaches himself for a small social failure. A smile, he reflects, would have sufficed in the moment.

The smallest response would have encouraged the other man to speak. Why, the narrator asks, had he not given it? A smile is not much to demand between human beings. He finds it pitiable that convention persuades us to withhold it. A fellow creature, perhaps in need, was refused that trifle. The tale builds its moral weight from that tiny chill. Readers get Sackville-West's fine, quiet prose on manners and regret.
22483-across-unknown-south-america:
Across Unknown South America records an expedition into little-known country. Its opening exchange shows how remote the goal seemed to outsiders. A cinematograph man marvels at the journey's length in amazement.

More than three months to reach the spot, he repeats. Then perhaps Monsieur is on a journey to Mars or the moon! He laughs heartily at his own wit on the spot. No place on earth, he insists, takes so long to reach. The travelers knew better and went anyway into the interior. Their account follows rivers, forests, and peoples rarely visited then. Readers get exploration writing with a camera crew along for the record.
22568-blue-aloes-stories-of-south-africa:
Cynthia Stockley wrote Blue Aloes, stories of South Africa, in 1919. Blue Aloes is a farm whose mistress knows the Karoo well. A night noise frightens a newcomer in the opening story's scene.

It was probably a stray ostrich pecking on your shutters, she says. You are strange to the Karoo, my dear, she adds kindly. When you have been here a month, you will notice nothing. Night noises will stop troubling you by then, she promises. Stockley's stories draw on settler life in dry, wide country. Love, loneliness, and farming hardship run through her South African tales. Readers get a woman writer's view of Karoo farms and folk.
22759-the-english-at-the-north-pole-part:
Jules Verne wrote The English at the North Pole, part one of The Adventures of Captain Hatteras, his novel of Arctic exploration. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Captain Hatteras, an Englishman obsessed with reaching the North Pole, fits out a brig at Liverpool and sails into the ice with a crew that does not know its destination.

The opening quotes the Liverpool Herald of April 1860, noting a brig's departure, an event of little importance for so great a port. Who would notice one vessel among the shipping crowding six miles of docks? Verne builds his epic from that shrug. Hatteras became the type of the polar monomaniac, and the novel, in two parts, is early Verne at full stretch.
348-hesiod-the-homeric-hymns-and-homeric:
This volume gathers Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and the lesser Homerica in English translation. Contents run from Works and Days and the Theogony through the Shield of Heracles and the Catalogues of Women. Hymns to Dionysus, Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, and Aphrodite follow.

An introduction covers the Boeotian and Ionic schools, the Trojan cycle, and the contest of Homer and Hesiod. Fragments, epigrams, and burlesque poems close the set, with a bibliography. The book gives readers the full archaic Greek shelf beyond Homer. It serves students and lovers of myth. Hesiod's farmer calendar still speaks to readers of work and seasons.
a-yellow-god-an-idol-of-africa:
H. Rider Haggard opens in a magnificent City of London office built of Aberdeen granite, seat of Sahara Limited, a scheme to water the desert and enrich its promoters. Sir Robert Aylward, baronet and member of Parliament, runs the company. His nephew Alan Vernon, an engineer with a conscience, breaks with the scheme and with his uncle.

The contents promise the yellow god itself, a golden idol of the Asiki people, Jeekie's tale, dwarf folk, a hall of the dead, and a gold house. Alan sails for West Africa to return the idol his uncle's agents stole. Haggard mixes City fraud with African adventure, and the idol's curse hangs over both worlds.
an-introduction-to-the-mortuary-customs-:
Dr. H. C. Yarrow prepared this study for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology, printed by the Government Printing Office at Washington in 1880, as the title page states. Director J. W. Powell's letter notes it is the third of a series meant to promote research among the North American Indians. Yarrow gathers reports on how the many peoples of the continent treated their dead.

The study sorts the customs by kind: burial in graves and mounds, scaffold and tree burial, cremation, and mummifying, with the mourning rites, feasts, and beliefs that went with each. Reports come from army officers, agents, and travelers across the continent. Yarrow's compilation, written in the terms of its time, preserves records of practices then fast disappearing.
bandelier-islands-titicaca:
Lake Titicaca and its sacred islands drew Bandelier south for his 1910 report. The Islands of Titicaca and Koati records his survey of the famed sites. In Inca belief, the sun itself was born on those shores.

Bandelier gives the shrines their first study with true care for method. He maps ruins, tests old claims, and weighs local lore with respect. The high lake, its boats, and its stone remains fill his notes. His fieldwork helped launch a real science of the Andes. Readers meet bold claims checked, at last, against stone and soil in the field. The report rewards slow, close reading.
burke-s-speech-on-conciliation-with-amer:
Burke's Speech on Conciliation with America presents Edmund Burke and his great parliamentary argument for settling with the American colonies, in an edition prepared for students by Sidney Carleton Newsom. Newsom, a teacher of English at Indianapolis, wrote the introduction for readers without a well stocked library, drawing on older editions and a bibliography he lists in full. The speech itself follows his framing chapters.

Contents pages lay out the study plan: the political situation, Burke as statesman, Burke in literature, topics for special reports, and then the speech with notes and an index. In the address, Burke urges Parliament to win the colonies back by concession rather than force, arguing from trade, distance, and the spirit of liberty in America. This printing serves the classroom: a classic piece of political persuasion, wrapped in the help a young reader needs to follow it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-africa:
Africa, a name of Phoenician origin, was first given by Romans to the territory around Carthage. It gradually spread to the whole Libyan territory Rome occupied. It was still understood in that sense in the eleventh century, when Leo IX wrote that after the Roman pontiff, Carthage's bishop stands first in Nubia and as Africa's chief metropolitan. Arabs then adopted the name, then medieval writers, until it came to cover the entire continent.

Africa spans about 12,000,000 square miles, about three times Europe and five times the United States without Alaska. It joins Asia only by the Suez Isthmus. Its shape is an irregular triangle, and its scarcity of bays and harbours seriously affected its history before steam. It rests on a rocky foundation forming an immense interior plateau, whence ranges like the Atlas branch off. The long entry moves from geography and peoples to missions and Islam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-cias:
Agostino Ciasca, in the world Pasquale, was an Italian Augustinian cardinal, born at Polignano a Mare, in Bari province, on 7 May 1835. He died at Rome on 6 February 1902. He took the Augustinian habit in 1856, made profession in 1857, and was ordained priest in 1858. Having perfected himself at Rome in philosophy, theology, and canon law, he devoted himself particularly to Oriental languages, especially Arabic and Coptic.

Exemplary in life and loyal to the church, he became dear to Leo XIII, who gave him confidence and entrusted him with several delicate missions. In his order he served as professor, prefect of studies, assistant general, and procurator general. Later he served at the Vatican Council as theologian and interpreter for Oriental bishops. His chief works include Coptic-Sahidic biblical fragments from the Borgia Museum and Tatian's Arabic gospel harmony, edited with a Latin translation in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvar-nunez-c:
Alvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, born at Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, has uncertain birth and death dates. His peasant family called themselves Alhaja until Las Navas de Tolosa, 1212. Turning the Arab position by a mountain pass, marked by a cow's skull, won them nobility. He joined Narváez's Florida expedition in 1526 as treasurer, one of four mainland survivors with two Spaniards and an Arab Moor.

Eight years roaming Louisiana and Texas coasts ended when his scant medicine and faith cures made him a renowned medicine man. After nine years they reached Sonora's Pacific coast, first Europeans across North America. He reached Mexico City in 1536, first European to see and describe the bison. La Plata governor from 1541, he was rebelled against in 1543, sent to Spain, and kept eight years in mild captivity. His Naufragios of 1542 and Comentarios of 1555 remain key sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-bas:
The Ambrosian Basilica at Milan was raised by its great fourth-century bishop St. Ambrose and consecrated in the year 386. Its present form rose in four different periods, three in the ninth century and the fourth in the twelfth, though the original church is gone. Ambrose's own writings and modern research still give a fair idea of the founder's church. The original edifice resembled Rome's great churches of its age.

The basilica's story turns on Ambrose's final victory over the Arian court faction, after which the people sought its consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-america:
America, the Western Continent or New World, holds three main divisions. North America runs from about 70 to 15 degrees north, Central America's isthmus narrows to thirty miles at Panama, and South America from 12 degrees north to 55 south. Animism underlies the Indian creed everywhere, fetishism its tangible form, and monotheism, a personal all-creating ruling God, nowhere existed. Five European nations chiefly settled the continent after Columbus: Spain, Portugal, France, England, and Holland in date order; Sweden's small colony lasted under seventeen years.

Spanish exploration's precious-metal mines were worked progressively through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, then faded. The peoples later fought through the Napoleonic period to secure independence. No sufficient data fix America's Catholic population; even the United States' usual 14,000,000 is a conjecture more or less accurate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-rocca:
Angelo Rocca founded Rome's Angelica Library. Born at Rocca, now Arcevia, near Ancona, in 1545, he died at Rome on 8 April 1620. At seven he was received into the Augustinian monastery at Camerino, hence also called Camers or Camerinus, and he studied at Perugia, Rome, and Venice. Padua made him a doctor in theology in 1577.

In 1579 he became secretary to the Augustinian superior-general, in 1585 he took charge of the Vatican printing office, and he supervised the planned Bible and Fathers' editions. He became sacristan in the papal chapel in 1595, and in 1605 titular Bishop of Tagaste in Numidia. Rome's Augustinian public library, formally established on 23 October 1614, keeps his name. Mainly through his efforts came the Vulgate edition published under Clement VIII. He also edited Egidio Colonna and Augustinus Triumphus, and wrote on the sacraments, Scripture, canonization, and bells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apiarius-of-s:
Apiarius, a priest of Sicca in Roman Africa, matters in history only because his appeal to Rome sparked a long dispute between Rome and Carthage over who controls church discipline. Deposed by Urbanus, bishop of Sicca, for serious misconduct, he appealed to Pope Zosimus, who found flaws in the bishop's procedure, ordered the priest restored, and had the bishop disciplined. A general synod at Carthage in May 418 then forbade clerics below bishop to appeal beyond the seas, meaning across the Mediterranean to Rome.

Opponents of the papacy later read African resentment in the case as a denial of papal supremacy, the doctrine of the pope's supreme authority. Apiarius became the classic example in anti-Roman controversy for a fifth-century rejection of papal control. The article presents the case as a disciplinary quarrel that grew into a lasting argument about African church freedom and Roman claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arca:
An arca was a box in which early Christians kept the Eucharist, the consecrated bread, in their homes. Cyprian tells of a woman who tried with unworthy hands to open her box holding the Lord's holy body. Fire issued from it the moment she touched it, and she could not open it. Wilpert believes a fresco in the catacomb of Saints Peter and Marcellinus shows such a box. It shows Christ seated reading from an open roll, three jars on his right, and on his left a square box filled with loaves, emblems of the Eucharist.

Arca also meant a receptacle for Christians' offerings for the church or the poor, cited from Tertullian and the Liber Pontificalis, the book of popes. The entry joins a devotional object and a charity chest under one Latin word, showing how early believers guarded the sacrament at home and gave for the common good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barca:
Barca was a titular see of Cyrenaica in northern Africa. Most archaeologists place it at Medinet el Merdja, though Graham puts it at Tolometa, or Tolmeita. Often destroyed and restored, it sank in the Roman period to a mere borough, yet still held a bishopric.

Its bishop Zopyros attended Nicaea in 325; Zephyrius is a mistaken form of his name. Zenobius and Theodorus appear in the subscriptions at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451. Three bishops across three councils are all the record preserves. The see must have vanished when Arabs conquered the Pentapolis in 643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of Braganca was born about 1200 and died on 1 July 1271. Studying at Padua, he received the Dominican habit from St Dominic himself. In 1248 he was appointed to the Cypriot see of Nemonicum, a city now unknown. In 1254 he was sent as legate to England and France, following Henry III to Paris. There France's king gave him a relic of the true Cross and a thorn from the Crown.

Alexander IV made him Bishop of Vicenza in 1256, where he endured the tyranny of Ezzelino, religion's notorious enemy. The persecution drew out his high pastoral qualities, and he built Vicenza's Dominican Church of the Crown to house his relics. He joined King Louis of France at Joppa, Sidon, and Acre during the crusading expedition. Venerated by the people and honored as Blessed, he also wrote scriptural commentaries and sermons.

Bartholomew of Lucca was a historian born at Lucca about 1227, who died about 1327. Entering the Dominicans young, he won St Thomas Aquinas's respect and friendship as disciple, confidant, and confessor. In 1272 he followed Thomas from Rome to Naples, learning of his master's death at Fossa Nuova in 1274. He became prior of his native convent in 1288 and of Santa Maria Novella at Florence in 1301.

At Avignon he served nine years as chaplain to cardinals, and John XXII made him Bishop of Torcello in 1318. A clash with Grado's patriarch over an abbess brought excommunication and exile in 1321, but peace returned him in 1323. His best-known Annales, covering 1061 to 1303 in terse sentences, was finished about 1307. He verified statements with care, though his age's uncritical temper let fables like Popess Joan stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-p:
Bartolommeo Pacca was a cardinal, scholar, and statesman, born at Benevento in 1756, who died at Rome in 1844. Schooled by Jesuits at Naples and at Rome's Clementine College, he became nuncio at Cologne in 1785, a center of anti-Roman agitation. Consecrated titular Archbishop of Damiata, he arrived in June 1786 to find Cologne, Trier, and Mainz refusing recognition unless he renounced jurisdiction.

Other bishops and Cologne's magistrates received him respectfully, and even Prussia made no difficulty. Frederick William honored him on the Rhine, and Rome accorded the Prussian monarch the royal title. His Cologne position stayed difficult, as Bonn's new university preached open war on the Holy See. His memoirs record acute observations on politics and history, including his Cologne nunciature and the years 1809 to 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilica:
Basilica is a word with two senses: a church's architectural style and its canonical status. In architecture it signifies a kingly, and secondarily beautiful, hall of Eastern origin, finest in Rome. Rome's Forum held basilicas of Porcia, Fulvia, Sempronia, and Opimia between 184 and 121 BC, then Caesar's Basilica Julia after 46 BC. They beautified the Forum and served markets and justice, open to the public and well lighted.

Vitruvius gives the usual plan: a parallelogram whose width runs between a third and a half of its length. Columns divide the middle space from a lower ambulatory as wide as the columns are high, with shorter upper columns admitting light. Canonically, basilica rank brings precedence over other churches, save the local cathedral, plus the conopaeum, bell, and cappa magna. The conopaeum, a red and yellow silk umbrella, is carried with the bell at the clergy's head on state occasions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardica:
Cardica was a titular see of Thessaly, the Latinized medieval form of Gardicium, truly Gardikion in Greek. It appears only in later see-lists from the 1100s or 1200s, under Larissa. Lequien names five Latin bishops from 1208 to 1389, beginning with Bartholomew, recipient of many letters from Pope Innocent III.

Lequien knew no Greek bishop of the see, but manuscript lists add eight names. They run from John in 1191 to Gregorius about 1852, with Metrophanes degraded in 1623 and Sophronius serving from 1646 to 1649. When Thessaly joined Greece in 1881 the see had stood vacant since 1875. It was suppressed in 1899, and Gardiki survives as a small town of about 3,000 people in the diocese of Phthiotis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-knig:
The Catholic Knights of America was a fraternal life-insurance company chartered under Kentucky law. Four Nashville men founded it. James J. McLoughlin led the group. D. N. Burke joined him, as did John Broderick and John McDonald. They first met on 23 April 1877 at Emmett Hall. The society began as the Order of United Catholics and later took its new name at Bishop P. A. Feehan's suggestion. Feehan, of Nashville, became its spiritual director.

Growth was rapid: sixteen branches met in the first supreme council at Louisville in July 1878, and seventy-two were represented at Indianapolis the next year. By 1 August 1907 the order counted 20,000 members in 560 branches across forty-two states. It had paid nearly fifteen million dollars to heirs of over 8,500 deceased members, and held resources of $828,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The Catholic University of America is a pontifical institution in Washington, D.C., comprising schools of Sacred Sciences, Philosophy, Law, Letters, and Science. Supreme authority rests with the Holy See, while governing power lies with the bishops of the United States, exercised through a board of trustees of bishops, priests, and laymen. The Archbishop of Baltimore serves as chancellor ex officio, and a rector, aided by an academic senate, runs the university day to day.

The desire for such a university was voiced at the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866 and took definite shape at the Third in 1884. By 1907 the university counted 32 teachers and 210 students, with a library of 100,000 volumes and its own quarterly, The Catholic University Bulletin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Mother of God of Lucca were founded by Blessed Giovanni Leonardi, born in 1541 at Diecimo in the Republic of Lucca. Sent to Lucca at seventeen to learn the apothecary's trade, he was piously inclined from childhood and was ordained on 22 December 1572. His congregation began in 1574, when two or three young laymen gathered round him for guidance in reforming manners and saving souls.

When his lay helpers prepared for priesthood and a religious order took shape, persecution broke out. The Fathers of the republic feared a native order spreading over Italy would expose the little state's affairs. Persecution kept Leonardi mostly banished from Lucca, admitted only by special Senate decree under papal pressure. In 1580 he secretly acquired Santa Maria Cortelandini, still held by his sons. Bishop Guidiccioni canonically erected the congregation in 1583 at Gregory the Thirteenth's instigation, confirmed by Clement the Eighth's brief of 13 October 1595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordia-in-:
Adolphus Ennis's entry covers the Diocese of Concordia in northwestern Kansas. Erected on 2 August 1887, it borders Colorado west, Nebraska north, and county lines east and south, across 26,685 square miles. In 1886 Leavenworth split into three sees: Leavenworth, Wichita, and Concordia. Richard Scannell of Nashville, nominated first bishop on 9 August 1887, ruled until 30 January 1891, when he moved to Omaha. Wichita's bishop then administered Concordia, and no new bishop came until 1897.

Growth followed fast. From 1898 to 1907, forty-five churches and twenty schools rose, besides new missions and stations. An 1884 boarding school for young ladies under the Sisters of Saint Joseph had led the way. By the time of writing, fifty-one secular and fifteen religious priests served ninety-one churches, thirty stations, and four chapels. Parochial schools held about 2,482 children, and academies at Concordia and Abilene about 135 pupils. The Catholic population stood at 26,125.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corsica:
Alexandre Guasco's entry covers Corsica, the Mediterranean's third island in size, surpassed only by Sicily and Sardinia. Antibes on the French Riviera lies one hundred and eleven miles from Calvi, Corsica's port nearest France. Brisk commerce runs between Leghorn in Italy and Bastia in Corsica, the voyage taking five hours. The island is mountainous and well watered, largely covered with forests and almost impenetrable thickets called maquis.

Coastal climate stays mild, while elevated regions run cold. Corsica's area measures 3,367 square miles, its population 300,000. Interior and coastal natives alike, descended from Italians, are nearly all Catholics. Phoenicians and Phocians early visited the island and established colonies there. For a time it belonged to Carthage. Christianity, it has been asserted, entered Corsica in Apostolic times. Before and after 600 the island stood in close dependence on the Apostolic See, and always remained so.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-sa:
The Council of Sardica, held most probably in 343, belongs to the series of councils wrestling with Arian doctrine and its fallout. Emperors Constans and Constantius convoked it at Pope Julius's urging, choosing Sardica, now Sofia, for a genuinely representative meeting. Athanasius and other bishops, condemned and vindicated by turns, awaited a final judgment.

Eastern bishops, in the minority, withdrew to act as a body, while the remainder refused to add to the Nicene Creed and enacted canons on bishops' transfers, trials, and appeals. Documents went to Pope Julius with a majority letter, yet pacification failed entirely, and the Eastern bishops grew bolder in defiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuenca:
A diocesan entry describes Cuenca, a suffragan see of Quito in Ecuador, created in 1779. Its episcopal city, 7,700 feet above sea level in a broad plain south-east of Guayaquil, holds 30,000 people, with Peruvian antiquities nearby. The diocese covers Azuay and Canar, and ranks second among Ecuadorian sees.

Jesuits led the first missions, followed by Franciscans, Dominicans, and others, working 130 successful years until the Society's expulsion in 1767. A Salesian mission now works eastward in Gualaquiza. The Franciscan Vicente Solano, famed as a controversialist, belonged to this diocese. Its organization owes most to Bishop Toral, who served from 1861 to 1883 and attended the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuernavaca:
A church entry covers Cuernavaca, set up in 1891 for the whole state of Morelos in Mexico. It is bounded by the archdioceses of Mexico and Puebla and the bishopric of Chilapa. It spans 7,184 square kilometres with 161,697 people, served in 34 parishes by 42 diocesan and 6 order priests.

Franciscans first preached the Gospel here, founding the Cuernavaca convent in 1526. Dominicans followed at Oaxtepec in 1529, and Augustinians at Ocuituco in 1534. By 1536, the Franciscan writer Motolinia claims, all the people had turned to the Faith. In the 1700s most churches passed from the orders to diocesan clergy. The first bishop, Fortino Hipolito Vera, was consecrated in 1894 and died four years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dacca:
A diocesan entry traces Dacca, a see in Bengal, India, from Portuguese jurisdiction to its own hierarchy. By a constitution of Paul III in 1534, Goa held spiritual rule from the Cape of Good Hope as far as China. Bengal's early Portuguese settlements fell under Goa. From 1606 they fell under Mylapore.

When British rule replaced Portugal, Mylapore still kept jurisdiction, and 7,000 of Dacca's 22,000 Catholics remained subject to it. For effective mission work, Propaganda made a Jesuit vicar apostolic of Calcutta and Bengal in 1834. Pius IX divided Bengal into two vicariates in 1850. A third followed in 1870. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-alvarez:
Diego Alvarez Chanca served as court physician to the Spanish sovereigns Ferdinand and Isabella. He sailed with Christopher Columbus on his second voyage to America in 1493. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry credits him with treating Columbus through a bout of malarial fever soon after landing in Haiti. He also saved other leaders of the expedition who fell sick.

On ground Chanca himself chose, the settlers raised Isabella, the first Christian town in the New World. It was named for the queen. His letter to the council of his home city, written after only three months on shore, stands as the first account of American plants, animals, and peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-capr:
Domenico Capranica was a cardinal, theologian, canonist, and statesman, born near Palestrina in 1400. At Padua and Bologna he studied canon and civil law brilliantly, winning the doctorate of both laws at twenty-one. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him as secretary to Martin the Fifth and apostolic prothonotary, made cardinal in secret in 1423 or 1426, though his rank was not proclaimed until 1430.

He earned swift rise by political and military service, ruling Imola and Forli and winning back rebellious Bologna. He became bishop of Fermo and played a part at the Council of Basle, of which he is said to have written a history never printed. His Rules of Life for a nephew, the entry notes, mirror a fine character. He died at Rome in 1458.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fabriano-and-:
Fabriano and Matelica form one diocese in central Italy, in the province of Macerata. Fabriano is famed for paper works and salted-fish trade. It is said to descend from refugees of ancient Attidium in the ninth century before Christ. Its baptismal font stayed at Attigio until 1254. Its story runs with the Marches.

San Benedetto holds the tomb of Blessed Giovanni Bonnelli, dead in 1290. Saint Silvestro Guzzoli, founder of that order, lies at Monte Fano nearby, and the relics of Saint Romuald moved to Saints Biagio and Romoaldo in 1480. Fabriano stood under Camerino until 1785, when Pius VI restored Matelica and joined it to Fabriano as equal heads. Matelica was a Roman colony from 89 before Christ, and its ancient bishops Equitius and Florentius are named. Gentile da Fabriano, the painter, was its most famed native.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-german-roman-:
The German Roman Catholic Central Verein of North America united German Catholic benevolent societies against secret societies and for Catholic rights. Its origin lies in 1854, when presidents of three Buffalo societies called German Catholic bodies together, urged by missionary priests and approved by Bishop Timon. A Mainz union of 1848 lent the model, and seventeen societies organized the Verein at Baltimore's Saint Alphonsus Hall on April 15, 1855.

Membership stayed limited to German-language Catholic benevolent societies, growing from seventeen societies and 1,500 members in 1855 to 548 societies and 48,989 members in 1895. A 1901 reorganization replaced direct local affiliation with state associations, and by 1907 sixteen state bodies and fifty-two locals counted 99,291 paid-up members. Pius IX praised the Verein in 1866, its fifty-two years gave about twelve thousand dollars to Peter's Pence, and its immigrant agents and Leo House in New York served newcomers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gioacchino-ve:
Gioacchino Ventura di Raulica was an Italian pulpit orator, patriot, and philosopher born at Palermo in 1792, who died at Versailles in 1861. He entered the Jesuits in 1808 and, when the order was suppressed in Sicily, joined the Theatines in 1817. Leo XII made him professor of canon law at the Sapienza, and in 1830 he became Superior-General of the Theatines. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his preaching and his politics in turn.

His eloquence, vehement and direct with a magnificent voice, won him renown in Rome and Paris, where he almost rivaled Lacordaire. Under Pius IX he glorified the union of religion and liberty. He defended the Sicilian Revolution, dreaming of an Italian confederation under the pope. After the Roman Republic fell in 1849 he withdrew to France, preached before Napoleon III, and closed his life as a moderate Traditionalist philosopher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista de Luca was a cardinal and Italian canonist of the seventeenth century, born at Venosa in southern Italy in 1614, who died at Rome in 1683. Born of humble parents, he studied at Naples, returned home in ill health, and went to Rome in 1645. There his legal skill won him a high reputation, along with much envy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a practical jurist of the Roman court.

Late in life he became a priest under the patronage of Innocent XI, who made him referendary, auditor of the Sacred Palace, and finally cardinal in 1681. His writings matter most for understanding the jurisprudence of the Roman court and the Rota of his day. His complete works, the Theatrum veritatis et justitiae, ran to nineteen volumes, with a later Cologne edition in twelve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-catholi:
Greek Catholics in America is an article on the Uniat churches of the Byzantine or Greek Rite, almost unknown in the United States some twenty-five years before 1909. Occasional priests from Syria came seeking aid, but their rite and peoples were wholly unknown to American Catholics. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the Slav immigration that changed that picture.

Emigration from the Slav lands of Austro-Hungary brought the Greek Rite in large numbers, with churches erected all over the country. The movement began about 1879 to 1880. Coal companies in Pennsylvania, terrorized by the Molly Maguires from 1871 to 1879, sought foreign labor abroad. The Austrian Slav, willing to work longer hours for less, succeeded in wage-earning, and his countrymen followed into the coal and iron districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-orthodo:
The Greek Orthodox Church in America is an article on those of the Greek Rite not in communion with the Holy See. Both sides share the official designation, but the dissenting churches stress Orthodox, correctness of doctrine, while the Uniat churches stress Catholic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows seven nationalities without unity or central obedience.

Nearly every city of size holds one or more churches of the communion. They conform to Byzantine usages but look to home Holy Synods for government. Seven nationalities use Old Slavonic, Greek, Arabic, and Rumanian as liturgical languages, and the Russian is the oldest and best established. Russian monks reached Alaska in 1793, built the first church on Kodiak Island in 1794, and converted many Eskimo and Indians before Alaska's sale in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huesca:
Huesca is a Spanish diocese in north-eastern Spain, covering parts of Huesca province, seven parishes in the Broto valley, and three parishes near Saragossa. Its origin cannot be fixed for certain: the earliest sure evidence is Bishop Gabinius signing Toledo's council decrees in 589. Isidore of Seville mentions an earlier bishop, Elpidius, but that testimony counts as less authoritative.

A synod at Huesca in 598 ordered yearly diocesan conferences and disciplinary measures. The Moorish invasion reached Huesca by 710, the city fell in 713, and the bishop fled, with the diocese run from Aragon. In 1063 the see moved to Jaca, staying there until Huesca was retaken in 1096 and Pedro I restored the original see. Later history ties Huesca closely to Barbastro, erected from its territory in 1571.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hungarian-cat:
Hungarian Catholics in America came from a kingdom whose people were far from all Magyar. The Kingdom of Hungary, separate from Austria except for foreign affairs, held Slovaks, Ruthenians, Rumanians, Slavonians, Croatians, Germans, and Italians alongside Hungarians proper, who barely formed a majority against all others combined. Immigrants from that kingdom were thus indiscriminately called Hungarians in America.

This article treats only immigrants of Hungarian race and language in the Roman rite, leaving Greek-rite Hungarians and other races to other articles. Their settlements lay scattered, usually in small numbers far apart, with only New York, Cleveland, Chicago, and Bridgeport large enough to support a church and priest. Magyar priests for mission work proved extremely hard to find, and dioceses tried various means to supply the lack.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hydatius-of-l:
Hydatius of Lemica, also called Idatius, was a chronicler and bishop. His birthplace was Lemica in Galicia, Ginzo de Limia in Spain today, late in the fourth century, and he died shortly after 468. As a child on a journey to Jerusalem he met St. Jerome. He entered clerical life around 417, and consecration as bishop followed in 427, probably for Aquae Flaviae, modern Chaves in Portugal.

Hydatius wielded political influence, shown when he went to Aëtius in Gaul in 431 to seek help against the Suevi. His Chronicle continues Jerome's work from 379 to 468. For its first part he draws on others' testimony, but from 427 onward he writes as a contemporary witness. Whether he also wrote the Fasti Consulares for 245 to 468, appended to the Chronicle, remains doubtful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isidore-of-th:

He ranked among the chief Eastern champions of reunion with Rome at the Council of Florence. His birth date is unknown and his people uncertain — described as Bulgar by some and Greek by others — though all his schooling was Greek.

At Constantinople he became a monk and abbot of St Demetrius. He was a man of unusually complete learning. He was strong in Latin, famed as a theologian, and a skilled orator. He was eager for reunion from the start. Constantinople, facing ruin by the Turks, weighed rescue by Western princes as the price of reunion, and in 1434 Isidore was sent to Basel. The entry follows a Greek churchman betting his career on East-West unity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaca:

It was once capital of the Jaccetani tribe named by Strabo. Its land saw battles between Sertorius and Pompey. Later it saw fighting between Pompey's son and Caesar's generals.

In church terms Jaca first belonged to Huesca's diocese. When Moors seized Huesca in 713, wandering bishops served the region. They lived at Jaca or in nearby monasteries. A council at Jaca in 1063 redrew Huesca's diocesan bounds. Those bounds later covered the present Huesca dioceses. The entry pairs mountain geography with a shifting church map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jamaica:

The nearest mainland point is about 400 miles southwest. Its name is said to come from Arawak words for water and wood, meaning a fertile land. The island runs 144 miles long and 21 to 49 miles broad.

Its area is 4,207 square miles, of which about 646 are flat alluvium, marl, and swamp. Copper is its most abundant mineral. The surface is very mountainous, with almost 2,000 square miles above 1,000 feet. Blue Mountain Peak rises 7,360 feet. Over two thousand plant and animal species are noted. The entry then covers history, peoples, government, and Catholic life on a sugar island of striking contrasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-ribeiro-:

As minister general, the order's worldwide head, he worked to restore discipline where it had grown lax, with a care praised for prudence and tact.

He founded a large library in the old Ara Coeli convent in 1740 and backed the Rome publication of Wadding's Annales Minorum in seventeen volumes between 1731 and 1741. Though he several times refused a bishopric, he at last accepted Oporto in 1741 on the nomination of King John V of Portugal.

female-suffrage-a-letter-to-the-christia:
Susan Fenimore Cooper addressed the Christian women of America in 1870 to argue against giving women the vote. Her letter ran in two parts in Harper's magazine. Cooper, daughter of novelist James Fenimore Cooper and a respected nature writer herself, grounded her case in scripture, history, and the duties of the home. first-footsteps-in-east-africa:

geological-observations-on-south-america:

Eight chapters move from the eastern coast's uplift to the western shore, where the Concepcion earthquake raised land before witnesses. Darwin then crosses the plains and valleys of Chile, noting salt crusts and a bed of nitrate of soda near Iquique. Pampas chapters describe giant fossil mammals, including mastodon bones, lying near shells of living species. Patagonian terraces, older Tertiary beds, and the split, folded rocks of the Cordillera fill the later pages. Geology students still read Darwin here as a field worker first, reasoning from cliffs, shells, and gravel rather than theory alone.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrewerJohnnyCal:

hesiod-the-homeric-hymns-and-homerica:

His Works and Days mixes farming counsel, fables, and hard wisdom about justice and labor, while his Theogony tells how the gods came to be, from Chaos to the reign of Zeus. The Shield of Heracles follows.

Then come the Homeric Hymns, long songs to gods such as Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, and Aphrodite, sung by bards who signed them with Homer's name. The last part, the Homerica, holds scraps of lost epics, the mock-heroic Battle of the Frogs and Mice, and the Contest of Homer and Hesiod. Together they open a window on the first age of Greek letters.
in-the-heart-of-africa:
Samuel White Baker's two great Nile books, The Nile Tributaries of Abyssinia and The Albert N'yanza, are condensed into this single volume by an editor signing only E. J. W. Baker, knighted and a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, explored the Sudan and the Nile basin in the 1860s. The contents open in the Nubian desert, at the bitter well, on the road to the Atbara river.

The chapters keep Baker's double subject: sport and discovery. Elephant and hippopotamus hunts, giraffe stalking, and a rhinoceros charge alternate with Khartoum, the slave trade, and a mutiny quelled at Gondokoro. Speke and Grant appear, fresh from the sources of the Nile. Kamrasi of Unyoro and the push toward the great lake close the journey. The condensation keeps the pace of a hunting diary and the argument of an explorer's report.
letters-from-america:
Rupert Brooke wrote these Letters from America after a journey begun in May 1913. He traveled through the United States, Canada, and the South Seas. He returned home in June of the next year.

The first thirteen chapters began as letters to the Westminster Gazette. Brooke meant to write a longer travel book later. War cut that plan short, and editors printed these pieces. Two chapters from the New Statesman close the volume. Readers meet a young poet's fresh eye on America. Brooke's wit made even shipboard and street scenes sparkle. His early death in war gave these letters added poignancy.
livingstone-missionary-travels-south-afr:
David Livingstone's Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa, published in 1857, tells his journeys of 1841 to 1856. Livingstone, a Scottish missionary and doctor, crossed the continent from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, the first European to do so. The book holds all 32 chapters of his account.

He describes the Kalahari, the Makololo kingdom, and his discovery of the great falls he named for Queen Victoria. His aims were mixed: preach the gospel, map the land, and open paths for honest trade against the slave trade. The book made him a national hero in Britain. It remains a vast storehouse on the peoples and geography of the interior.
miss-sarah-jack-of-spanish-town-jamaica:
Anthony Trollope published this tale in his 1864 collection Tales of All Countries. It opens with a melancholy essay on Jamaica's decline. The island, once fortune's favorite, has seen its sun set, Trollope writes. Yet he calls her scenery the gem of the western tropics, all green valleys and rapid rivers.

The hero, Maurice Cumming, is a sugar-grower near the Blue Mountain country. He inherited the Mount Pleasant estate at eighteen, after his father's death. Struggle, failure, and desolation had marked the family for years. Against this ruined planter's world, Trollope sets the romance of Miss Sarah Jack of Spanish Town.
mr-bonaparte-of-corsica: John Kendrick Bangs wrote this comic novel about Napoleon Bonaparte, the Corsican who became emperor of France. Bangs was America's leading literary humorist of his day, and this is the fifth of his books in the Gutenberg series. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the novel itself. It contains only the Project Gutenberg header, naming the title and author. Readers therefore get the book's identity and its famous subject, but the sample offers none of Bangs's jokes or scenes.
nasa-tm-19650018730-sa-10-flight-mechani:
Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory issued this flight mechanical summary for Saturn I vehicle SA-10 on July 13, 1965. SA-10 was to launch from Pad 37B at the Eastern Test Range. Its payload joined an Apollo boilerplate capsule, BP-9, with a Pegasus C meteoroid satellite. A spent upper stage would enter orbit with them.

The summary presents the predicted path for the flight. It also sets out the orbital goals of the mission. The planned orbit was circular, at about five hundred thirty-five kilometers up. Flight summaries like this one gave all teams one agreed picture before launch day arrived.
nasa-tm-19660001385-theory-of-low-energy:
Richard J Drachman at Goddard wrote this theory paper on what happens when a positron strikes a helium atom at low energy. A positron is the antimatter twin of the electron. At low energy, the pair may briefly join, but the study stays below that threshold. The catalog note says an adiabatic method is applied to the problem.

Scattering theory predicts how the positron is deflected. Helium is a simple, clean target for such tests. Exact results there check the methods used for harder atoms. Drachman's work belongs to basic atomic physics done inside a space agency, where such calculations also support the reading of spectra from space instruments.
nasa-tm-19670006720-effect-of-molecular-:
Mary H. Fowler, of the Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on November 14, 1966. It continues a study of how well polyaryloxy silane plastics stand up to heat. Fowler asks how changing the molecules' structure changes the materials' physical traits, above all their thermal stability.

Several new starting compounds were prepared from a family of aromatic diols, then purified by distillation and hydrolysis. Reacting the purified diols produced diphenyl aryloxy silane polymers with relatively high heat resistance. Every member of the group kept at least 48 percent of its weight when heated in nitrogen to 900 degrees Celsius. One polymer, built on a diphenylmethane linkage, kept 90 percent of its weight up to 566 degrees and matched the best material reported earlier.
nasa-tm-19670012066-thermal-radiation-fr:
John R. Howell, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a national heat transfer conference in Seattle, Washington, in August 1967. It examines a standard shortcut in radiation calculations. The assumption is local thermodynamic equilibrium. It treats each small pocket of gas as settled and balanced so its temperature can be defined.

Howell asks what happens to calculated thermal radiation when that assumption fails. The case he studies is a gas with too few collisions between particles to redistribute absorbed radiation energy. Then the energy states cannot hold their equilibrium pattern, and the emitted radiation no longer follows the usual spectral distribution. Using the simple case of a grey gas, he derives rough relations. They mark the conditions where such shifts away from equilibrium should be expected.
nasa-tm-19670021973-some-vector-generati:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this paper in June 1967 on early computer graphics hardware. It presents vector generating techniques for cathode ray tube display systems. Vector displays draw pictures as lines rather than as a scanned image, so each line segment must be generated by dedicated circuitry.

Many display systems of the day could draw letters and numbers but had no vector generator for graphic information. Anyone needing line drawing faced a buy-or-build decision with little published guidance. The report answers with a general discussion of vector generating techniques for non-scan displays. It explains how digital position data flows through converters and amplifiers to the tube's deflection circuits. Two straightforward line drawing schemes are then described in detail, giving readers a basis for choosing or building a generator.
nasa-tm-19680025669-effects-of-several-r:
James L. Hunt and Robert A. Jones of Langley Research Center tested Apollo command module heating at Mach 8 in this 1968 report. Several ramp, fairing, umbilical, and pad configurations were compared in the Langley variable-density hypersonic tunnel. Protrusions near the capsule's base can sharply raise local heating during entry.

Tests covered three angles of attack and two flow densities. Ramp-fairing-umbilical setups cut the area of high interference heating at the umbilical base substantially. Peak interference heating, however, showed no significant reduction. A simulated wire bundle case lowered peak heating at the umbilical base. The highest heating rates appeared at the shear and compression pads. Those rates reached several times the stagnation point value.
nasa-tm-19700033380-permanent-impact-def:
Richard E. Morris of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in October 1970. It studies the lasting dents that impacts leave in spherical shells. Such shells form the walls of tanks and of containment vessels for nuclear reactors.

Morris gathered published test data from many past impacts. He then fit the data with a single correlation equation built on dimensional analysis. The equation ties the dent size to the shell material, the impact speed, and the shell's size and wall thickness. The data came from small shells, from under an inch to a few inches across. Designers could use the fit to predict damage from a strike.
nasa-tm-19700033856-directions-and-impli:
Perry W. Kuhns of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a November 1970 symposium in Oxfordshire, England. The meeting treated the new communication technology and what it means for society. Kuhns ties the growth of the field to NASA's own development programs.

The areas he discusses reach across the field. They include low-cost receivers for space broadcasting and high-efficiency microwave tubes. He also covers solid state transmitters, shaped antenna beams, and laser communications. Information storage and retrieval and orbit and frequency questions close the list. The paper asks where these gains point in the years ahead.
new-chronicles-of-rebecca:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote New Chronicles of Rebecca as a set of eleven linked tales about a girl named Rebecca. Headings call each part a chronicle. The first is Jack O'Lantern, and the second is Daughters of Zion. A verse by Francis Turner Palgrave opens the tales, praising a child's sweetness.

Rebecca's thought book forms the third chronicle, and a tragedy in millinery the fourth. Later parts cover the saving of the colors, the State of Maine girl, and a little prophet. Abner Simpson's new leaf and Rebecca's own memories close the set. Village life in Maine, seen through a bright girl, holds the tales together.
parkman-jesuits-north-america:
Parkman told the Jesuit story in The Jesuits in North America, from 1867. The book forms Part Two of France and England in North America. Brébeuf, Jogues, and the Huron martyrs stand at its brave center.

Parkman drew his tale straight from the Jesuit Relations themselves. He shapes their reports into a swift, gripping work of narrative art. Faith, hunger, torture, and hope mark the black robes' hard road. A Protestant author treats Catholic heroes with awe and respect here. The book remains the most read telling of the French missions in North America. Its heroes live on in the minds of countless readers since.
people-of-africa: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the production notes of the electronic edition of People of Africa, with no page of the book itself visible. The notes say the edition follows the 1921 printing, published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and in New York by Macmillan, and name Edith A. How as the author. They record two small misprints the editor corrected, on a sandstorm and a single word in chapter four.
pinocchio-in-africa:
Eugenio Cherubini sent Carlo Collodi's wooden puppet on a new adventure in Pinocchio in Africa, translated from the Italian by Angelo Patri, a New York school principal. The book appeared in 1911 with original drawings by Charles Copeland.

The contents trace a wild trip in short chapters: Pinocchio skips school, visits a circus, makes friends with wild animals, and resolves to go to Africa. There he eats dates, spends his first night, is well received, is arrested, sells drinking water, rides on a dog's back, and travels with a caravan. He is even offered for sale before the journey ends. Young readers get the puppet's mischief in a new and stranger setting.
podcast-dannyjones-roqeyidYpcA:
Former NSA official Tom Drake joins Danny Jones to tell what he calls the darkest secrets of the deep state. Drake blew the whistle on NSA waste and spying and paid for it in court. He speaks as a true insider.

Drake tells how the state grew its watch net after the 2001 attacks and how it turned on its own staff. He warns that the tools now watch all of us. Jones asks what Drake would tear down first. Listeners get a grave talk from a man the state once charged. The library files it as an archive record of his account.
podcast-joerogan-Hc6pbG4wICA:
Investigative reporter George Knapp and filmmaker Jeremy Corbell join episode 1510 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Knapp has covered Area 51 and Bob Lazar since 1989, when he first put Lazar on TV. Corbell makes films from the same beat. Together they are the press wing of UFO disclosure.

They present the evidence they rate highest and describe how they work sources inside the secret world. Rogan asks what they cannot yet prove and why officials leak in hints. The episode is a strong sample of UFO journalism from its two most persistent practitioners, part history lesson and part status report.
podcast-joerogan-Wwp1BFEw3cA:
Brothers Jeremie and Edouard Harris, founders of the AI safety firm Gladstone, join Joe Rogan for episode 2311. The twins have briefed governments on the risks of advanced AI. Their message is a warning: the machine age may be moving faster than anyone's control.

The brothers explain how AI systems could escape oversight and why labs race ahead anyway. They describe the reports they wrote for the US government on worst-case paths. Rogan asks what ordinary people should watch for as the tech spreads. Tech-wary and curious listeners get two brothers making one urgent case together.
rosa-alchemica:
W. B. Yeats tells this tale of the alchemists in the first person, under a line from Euripides on those who know the mysteries of the gods. His narrator has just published a little work, Rosa Alchemica, in the manner of Sir Thomas Browne. Believers in the arcane sciences wrote to upbraid his timidity.

More than ten years have passed since he last met Michael Robartes and his fellow students, and saw their tragic end. The narrator had found the alchemists' doctrine no mere chemical fancy, but a philosophy of universal change toward a divine substance. His book made it a reverie on the changing of life into art, and his Dublin rooms were dressed to match.
saracinesca:
F. Marion Crawford published Saracinesca in 1887, after earlier novels that include Mr. Isaacs and Zoroaster. A short note before the story explains the title. Crawford worried the name might belong to an old Roman family title that no one still used. To stay safe, the magazine version added one letter and printed the name as Sarracinesca in Blackwood's Magazine. Later checks showed the shorter form was free, so the book brings that spelling back.

The story opens in Rome in 1865, a city the narrator presents as largely unchanged and not yet rebuilt. Readers meet streets, riverbanks, and open ground as they stood before later road work reshaped them. French soldiers fill the streets alongside Papal Zouaves. Coaches carry cardinals through the crowds, and mounted guards ride along the Corso. That crowded, ceremonial city forms the setting for the novel that follows.
scotland-s-mark-on-america:
George Fraser Black wrote this short history, issued in New York in 1921 by the Scottish Section of America's Making, with a foreword by John Foord. Black traces how Scots and their children shaped the United States, from early settlement in the colonies through high national office.

Chapters name Scots who served as colonial governors, signers of the founding declaration, presidents, vice presidents, cabinet members, senators, and judges. Later pages cover Scots in the army and navy. Readers get a proud roll of names and posts that shows one small nation's wide reach in American public life.
shenandoah-a-military-comedy-representat:
Bronson Howard (1842-1908) wrote this military comedy, presented in a series of representative American plays. An editor's opening pages recall Howard through his letters to Brander Matthews, full of sage comment and native wit. The editor praises Howard's noble character and sound mind.

A memorial volume from the American Dramatists Club in 1910 gathered tributes, yet the letters, the editor holds, show the true man best. Howard's earlier plays may fade, the editor grants, while Shenandoah keeps his name. The Civil War comedy of love and divided duty stands as his best-known stage work.
south-america: W. H. Koebel wrote South America for the series The Making of the Nations, with thirty-two full-page pictures from photos and maps and plans in the text. Adam and Charles Black printed the London book in MCMXIII, that is, 1913. A front picture shows Christopher Columbus, from the portrait in the Metropolitan Museum of Art at New York. The contents open with the continent in pre-Spanish days, then Columbus, the Spanish conquistadores, and the finding and early past of Brazil.
the-argonautica: Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica is present in R. C. Seaton's English version, dated 1912, through a detailed summary of Book One. Seaton was once a fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge. The summary opens with a call on Phoebus and the cause of the voyage. It then lists the Argonauts one by one. Jason parts from his mother Alcimede, and the Argo is launched. Idmon foretells what is to come. Idas behaves badly at the feast, and Orpheus sings. The book ends with Lemnos, Cyzicus, and Heracles left behind.
the-black-man-s-place-in-south-africa:
Peter Nielsen published an argument at Cape Town and Johannesburg in 1922, dedicated to his mother. In a preface he claims the standing of an observer who studied South Africans on the spot for many years. He says he learned their speech at first hand, not through interpreters.

A first section states the question in terms of white rule. Whites, he writes, have carried that burden alone, sure of their fitness, and have seen black people as fit only for service. Yet signs of growing strength and racial self-awareness now disturb that view. Nielsen's own racial framing is of its period and is stated plainly at the start.
the-camp-fire-girls-at-long-lake-or-bess:
Jane L. Stewart wrote The Camp Fire Girls at Long Lake, or Bessie King in Summer Camp, volume three of the Camp Fire Girls Series. The Saalfield Publishing Company put it out in 1914. A plate shows Dolly bound to a tree, a handkerchief over her mouth. Chapter I is called A Groundless Jealousy.

Dolly Ransom, a black-haired, mischievous Wood Gatherer of the Manasquan Camp Fire, speaks first. She and Zara sit on a wagon half filled with new-mown hay, at the farm of Zara's guardian, Miss Eleanor Mercer, called Wanaka. Enemies had kept her from them, till the shrewd suspicions of Bessie King, Zara's best chum, exposed a faithless friend. Below the wagon two more girls, in middy blouses and wide blue bloomers, toss up the hay. Walter Stubbs, one of the farm boys, directs the work with amusement.
the-congo-and-coasts-of-africa: Richard Harding Davis, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, wrote The Congo and Coasts of Africa. It was printed in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1907 with photos by the author and others. Its contents list five chapters, moving from coast traders and a piece called My Brother's Keeper to the Congo capital, Americans in the Congo, and hunting hippos. Davis dedicates the book to Cecil Clark Davis, his fellow traveler on the voyage. Only the front matter and contents are present here.
the-contest-in-america:
John Stuart Mill wrote The Contest in America on the American Civil War, reprinted here from Fraser's Magazine. He begins with relief. For a month a dark cloud had hung over the civilized world. It raised fears that Britain and the United States, the only two first-rate powers that were also free nations, would go to war with each other.

Mill says Britain had truly been wronged and had to respond, yet a war on America's side would have backed slavery. He reminds readers of Britain's record against the slave trade, bought with vast sums spent blockading the African coast. A war for the South would have helped set up a slave republic. Its builders broke from the Union to spread slavery. The essay weighs how a nation with such a record could act without betraying its own stated aims.
the-englishwoman-in-america:
Isabella Lucy Bird's The Englishwoman in America comes with a foreword and notes by Andrew Hill Clark. Her contents promise a brisk tour. Heads name the voyage out and a first view. Then come an unwelcome reception, Halifax and the Blue Noses, and bad roads. A tea dinner and a night ride to a Highland cabin close the first run. Later heads reach Prince Edward Island, the garden island, with its politics, gossip, and servant troubles.

Bird crossed the Atlantic in 1854 and wrote with a sharp, funny eye. Young, ill, and keen, she turned rough travel into a hit book. It launched a life of famed travel writing.
the-french-in-the-heart-of-america:
John Finley wrote The French in the Heart of America from talks first given at the Sorbonne in Paris and in many French towns. The book tells what French pioneers did in the Mississippi Valley.

Finley hoped to wake French pride in that past and to show Americans the brave ground their lives stand on. The great war broke in as the book went to press, filling the rooms of scholars with wounded men. He owns his chief debt to Parkman, whose tale of France in America guides these pages. From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf, French priests, traders, and soldiers first mapped the heart of the continent.
the-poetical-works-of-john-dryden-volume:
Volume I of The Poetical Works of John Dryden, issued in 1855 with life, critical dissertation, and notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan, opens with Dryden's biography. He was born on August 9, 1631, at Aldwincle in Northamptonshire, the eldest of fourteen children. His family came from Cumberland. One ancestor gained the estate of Canons-Ashby by marriage with a daughter of Sir John Cope.

The life traces both parents' Puritan connections, which Dryden later made his name by opposing. His mother was Mary Pickering, whose family had suffered in the aftermath of the Gunpowder Plot. Schooling began at Tichmarsh or Oundle, accounts differ. It became certain at Westminster, where Dryden was a king's scholar under Dr. Busby. Busby saw the boy's poetical power early and encouraged him to write. Gilfillan follows the family line in detail before turning to the poems themselves.

Volume II of The Poetical Works of John Dryden, issued in 1855 with life, critical dissertation, and notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan, opens with a critical estimate of Dryden's genius. Its first question is how far a poet's writings, their morals and their taste, should be judged by the character of his own age. Gilfillan warns readers away from extremes on either side.

Judging an older book's taste by modern rules, he argues, is like judging ancestral dress by present fashion. Morality needs the same allowance. Offences against decorum differ before and after the spread of the Christian code. Genius, he writes, often laboured in chains to its own tradition and period. It lacked the higher models later ages enjoy. That plea for historical fairness frames his examination of the varied fruits of Dryden's talent.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Medical Poems form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes in the 1893 three-volume set. The section gathers verse from the medical world. Titles include The Morning Visit, The Two Armies, and The Stethoscope Song. A poem for the American Medical Association meeting at New York on May 5, 1853, appears. So does Rip Van Winkle, M. D.

The Morning Visit opens the section. A sick man's chamber, the poem jokes, can hardly claim the right to propose a health. Friendship must still launch a sentiment, as a prisoned damsel tosses a kiss from her fingertips. The morning visit's mystery, Holmes says, is only learned when the visitor becomes the patient. Charging a neighbour a fee for showing him your face is a small matter. Lying helpless while friends write recipes is quite another, since then your own ox is gored.
the-red-man-s-continent-a-chronicle-of-a:
Ellsworth Huntington explains in his preface to the 1919 Yale volume that geography shapes the history he tells. He stresses the matching forms of the Old and New Worlds, the spread of native plant life in North America, and the effect of climate on health and energy.

Huntington gives special weight to how land and climate pressed on Indigenous peoples who lacked iron tools, draft animals, and any grain but corn. Proof is shortened for general readers, who are warned not to judge conclusions before seeing fuller work elsewhere. The book offers an early, readable attempt to read aboriginal America through environment.
the-rover-of-the-andes-a-tale-of-adventu:
R. M. Ballantyne's The Rover of the Andes is dated 1885. Its first chapter is set at the foot of the mountain range. The day is bright and warm. The events lie fifty or sixty years in the past. A solitary traveller rides a little mule. He climbs slowly up the western slopes of the Andes.

The man is huge, loose-limbed, and long-legged. A soft flaxen beard frames his face. He wears a grey hunting coat and a broad sombrero. Pistols hang in his belt, with a cavalry sabre at his side. Yet his face shows deep kindness. He never actually strikes the mule. When the animal refuses to be led, he laughs and rides on. At a rocky eminence he watches two riders approach. One is a Spanish-looking man. The other is an Indian girl.
veronica: Johanna Spyri wrote Veronica and Other Friends, two stories for children. Louise Brooks rendered them from the German. De Wolfe, Fiske and Company issued the book at Boston, with copyright in 1886. The pages given here hold the title page and the contents of Veronica only, so the stories themselves are not shown. Eleven chapters carry Veronica from a visit to the doctor through fresh courage. A jump of nine years, unsafe paths, and advice from lame Sabina follow. The last chapter says the motto proves true.
wanderings-in-south-america:
Charles Waterton offers his Wanderings in South America with a hesitating hand, in a preface to the first edition. The book has little merit, he fears. It must make its way through the world as well as it can, taking many a jostle. It may even join the slain in the field of modern criticism. Even in death it might serve him. Some chance rover, turning its pages, could catch the idea of exploring Guiana.

If such a reader gives the world a fuller account of that noble country, Waterton will claim a share of his honors. He was the first mover of those discoveries, as Ulysses sent Achilles to Troy. He had meant to write at far greater length, but years passed and nothing was done. So the account goes forth as written at the time. Guiana's birds, beasts, and river journeys stay fresh in it.
what-prohibition-has-done-to-america:
Fabian Franklin wrote What Prohibition Has Done to America, copyrighted in 1922 by Harcourt, Brace. His chapter list names the charges at once: bending the Constitution, making lawbreakers, and harming the federal system. Later chapters ask how the amendment passed and how lawmakers treat their own law.

Franklin opens by saying a constitution guards the basics of rule from quick change by a bare majority. The founders, he notes, meant to bind later voters on those basics. From that ground he attacks the ban on drink as a misuse of the frame. Readers get a clear, sharp brief against Prohibition in its early years.
white-queen-of-the-cannibals-the-story-o:
A. J. Bueltmann wrote White Queen of the Cannibals, the story of Mary Slessor of Calabar. The first chapter opens in Scotland, where Mother Slessor tells her children about Nigeria. Calabar, she says, is a dark land where the gospel light shines weakly. Many people there, she warns, eat other people.

Little Mary asks if missionaries work there at all. Her mother says a few do fine work, but thousands have never heard one. The contents trace Mary's path: a drunkard's home, a brave girl, work in Africa, and trips into the jungle. Witchcraft, a poison test, and wins for Mary fill later chapters. Faith and courage carry the tale.
